title: The Proud Queen City Brought Low
overview: This chapter is a mocking poem against Babylon, the empire that conquered Jerusalem, announcing that its cruelty and arrogance will end in sudden collapse.

parts.label: Off the throne, into the dust (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Babylon is pictured as a pampered royal young woman forced to sit in the dust like a mourner, grind grain like a slave, and wade rivers with her legs bared. This was the humiliating treatment war captives often suffered, and God says it will now fall on Babylon.

parts.label: Who stands behind this (v. 4)
parts.note: A short line names Israel's Redeemer (a relative who steps in to rescue family) as the LORD of hosts, the Holy One of Israel. Scholars are unsure whether this is the prophet or the people breaking in with praise, or simply an introduction to God's next words.

parts.label: Why Babylon is judged (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: God says he let Babylon conquer his people as punishment, but Babylon went far beyond that, showing no mercy and loading heavy burdens even on the elderly. Sure she would rule forever, she never stopped to think how it might end.

parts.label: Claiming to be God (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Babylon says, "I am, and there is none besides me," words this part of Isaiah uses for God alone, and feels sure she will never be a widow (lose her king) or childless (lose her people). The poem says both will happen in a single day, and no ritual or payment will turn it away.

parts.label: Daring the star readers (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: With open sarcasm, the poem challenges Babylon's famous magicians and astrologers, who read the stars and new moons for omens, to save the city if they can. They will burn like dry straw in a fire too fierce to warm anyone, and those Babylon relied on will scatter.

disagreement: Some Christians read this chapter mainly as a word about the historical city of Babylon, while others also see Babylon as a lasting picture of proud, oppressive world power, as the New Testament book of Revelation later does.
think: When a person or a nation comes to believe nothing can ever touch them, how do you think that changes the way they treat the people under their power?
